question: As the owner, I want a crew member's checklist answers to land in the database my reports and payroll read, so that a shift's work is never silently lost between the phone and the books. Which shape delivers that — (i) the Supabase substrate becomes the truth source, (ii) build a substrate→HQ propagation path, or (iii) split reads from writes so RxDB serves reads and HQ's REST path keeps owning writes?
proposal: (iii) Split reads from writes — RxDB serves reads, HQ's REST path keeps owning writes. The operator waives P-KR3's parallel-run prohibition for this shape only; a build WO still may not propose it.

votes.note: Delivers the user-visible value the widening was bought for — the two-device live list — while making the silent-empty-submit failure structurally impossible. The cost is admitting the hard swap was scoped before the two-server topology was settled, which is a planning correction rather than a product loss.

The only shape that is a card rather than a milestone. (i) fans into four-plus repoint cards and adds a hard runtime dependency; (ii) has no conflict rule and would park at G6 on a design question. (iii) can be slated tonight against a known footprint.

Measured, not argued: RxDB replicates to a second Postgres, the 0002 bridge is HQ→substrate read-only carrying permissions not data, and nothing carries a row back. Retiring /saveResponse detaches answers from submission and the card's own done_when: would pass while data is lost. Same-transaction write to both is already proven impossible (max_prepared_transactions = 0 both ends).

weighing: No adopted preference speaks to this question — the folder has process P-1..P-4 (test determinism) and constitutional P-1..P-6 (escalation ceilings), none of which bear on where a write lands. Recorded with no citation deliberately rather than stretching one to fit; this is a genuine coverage gap and belongs on the next evening's offer-back shortlist. The answer was captured as pending candidate architecture/C-3 precisely to close it.

question: As a crew member splitting a shift, I want to see the opening checklist my colleague already completed, so that I don't redo it or assume it was skipped. At cutover, do they still see it — accept the narrowing to their own assigned templates, keep the list tabs on REST, or add a fifth read policy row?
proposal: Nothing narrows — both list tabs stay on REST as a consequence of F-1's read/write split. B-61 closes.

votes.note: A product rule about who sees whose work is the operator's, not a card's. Worth naming that HQ's team-wide visibility was never a deliberate authorization decision — it exists only as a code comment in repository.go — so the fork was as much about making it explicit as about changing it.
Resolves for free under F-1's answer, so it costs no card. Had F-1 gone to (i) or (ii) this would have needed either a release note or decision 111 reopened.

Not a security finding — the substrate is strictly tighter — and explicitly not fixable by widening scope.templateIds, since the refusal is the server's (checklist_submissions_select is hq_can_see_template). With lists on REST the substrate predicate never applies to a list render.

weighing: No adopted preference bears on a visibility product rule. Recorded uncited rather than stretching constitutional P-1, which governs amending signed artifacts, not product semantics.
reasons: top-severity questions are the operator's — no number of citations clears them

question: As the owner, I want the sales-processor maintainer to hear about our contract errors in a way that reads as one honest correction rather than a drip of separate apologies, so that they trust the numbers we send them afterwards. Do the two owed notices go together or separately — hold to decision 106's two-notice sequencing, amend it and send one combined notice, or send P6's and retire A1's?
proposal: Amend decision 106 and send one combined notice covering both contract documents and all 111 audited rows. Nothing sends until the B3/B4/B6-B10 corrections are made and the operator has read the corrected draft.

votes.note: Outward-facing and irreversible — sending is the operator's act by definition, and the card was deliberately scoped to stop short of it. The trust argument favours one complete correction: a notice describing one drifted row, followed days later by one describing 45 wrong rows, reads as concealment even when it is not.

Amending 106 is cheaper than executing it: A1's notice was never drafted, so holding to the sequencing means drafting a second notice whose content the combined one already covers, and doing so while knowing it carries an error the audit found.

Verified at triage by searching all of git history with --diff-filter=A: exactly one notice file has ever existed in this repo, P6's. The draft's own claim that A1's was 'drafted 2026-08-01' is false and is B3 on the fix-forward list. A1's :31/A10 attributes a timezone claim to /menu-cogs, which contains no AT TIME ZONE.

cited.statement: changing the content of a signed slate, PRD, or sign-off table after you approved it escalates rather than being amended in place.
cited.weight: strong — this is the ceiling, not a leaning.
cited.fit: P-1 holds that changing what you approved escalates rather than being amended in place. Decision 106 is a recorded ruling rather than a signed slate, so the fit is by analogy, not by letter — but the behaviour P-1 prescribes is exactly what happened: the run escalated the sequencing as fork F-3 instead of quietly amending 106 itself. Cited to record that the escalation was correct, not to claim P-1 decided the answer.

weighing: The single citation constrains HOW the question had to be handled (escalate, do not amend in place), not WHICH option to choose. Nothing in the folder speaks to notice sequencing or counterparty communication on the merits, so the substance was decided on the evidence P6's audit produced rather than on any standing leaning. That gap is real and is why the answer was captured back as pending candidate process/C-1.
reasons: top-severity questions are the operator's — no number of citations clears them
